name: Nasal valve repair

card.summary: Functional surgery to widen or support the narrowest part of the nasal airway when it collapses; the literature is mostly case series with improvements reported.
card.note: A breathing operation first; appearance changes can accompany it.

quick.overview:
The nasal valve is the narrowest part of the nasal airway. When its walls are weak or narrow, the nostrils can collapse inward on inhalation. Nasal valve repair covers surgical ways of supporting or widening it, often with cartilage grafts or sutures.

It appears in looksmaxxing discussion mainly as a breathing fix that overlaps with nose shaping.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons typically add structural support, for example spreader or batten-type grafts, or use minimally invasive implants, sometimes alongside septoplasty and turbinate surgery. Diagnosis often involves the Cottle manoeuvre, though its accuracy has been questioned.
quick.risks: A 25-year systematic review found supportive evidence for valve surgery but limited by study quality. Complications are those of nasal surgery in general, including persisting obstruction and the possibility of revision.

lead: Nasal valve repair refers to surgical techniques that treat obstruction caused by compromise of the nasal valve, the narrow region of the airway at the junction of the upper lateral cartilage, septum and turbinate. It is a form of functional rhinoplasty, performed first to improve breathing.[1][2]

The appearance link is that the grafts and sutures used to hold the valve open also reshape the nose. In a retrospective series of 53 patients, spreader grafts widened the middle third of the nose and alar batten grafts softened deep alar creases and widened the tip, so surgeons treat the airway and the outward shape together.[2] Patients who already want a cosmetic rhinoplasty can have valve support planned alongside it.[3]

A 25-year systematic review found that 44 studies met its inclusion criteria, most of them level 4 evidence, and that all generally supported the effectiveness of functional rhinoplasty for obstruction from valve collapse.[1] Reviews of the field note that high-grade controlled trials comparing methods are scarce.[5]

paras: The nasal valve is the narrowest part of the airway. The internal valve lies between the upper lateral cartilage and the septum, and the external valve is formed by the flexible lower lateral cartilage and nostril rim.[3] Collapse of either, on inhalation, can feel like a blocked nose despite an open septum.

Because the valve regions give the nose its mid-vault width and nostril shape, repair changes outward appearance as well as airflow. In the 53-patient series, the authors assessed the cosmetic effect from postoperative photographs and described the mid-third widening produced by spreader grafts and the nasal-tip widening and alar-crease effacement from alar batten grafts.[2] In that series the most common cause of obstruction was previous rhinoplasty.[2]

A general rhinoplasty reference describes the internal valve as bounded by the upper lateral cartilage, septum, nasal floor and the head of the inferior turbinate, and the external valve as depending on the lower lateral cartilage. A valve angle above roughly 15 degrees is described as generally needed for unobstructed breathing.[3]

The Cottle manoeuvre, in which the cheek is pulled laterally during inspiration, is used to test for valve collapse. A 2020 study evaluated its validity and specificity, and the general reference notes false positives can occur.[4][3]
Overviews discuss diagnosis and treatment and innovations in nasal valve surgery.[5][6]

Reports describe grafts to widen or support the valve, and a minimally invasive repair evaluated with the NOSE scale.[7] A computational fluid dynamics study modelled the effect of individual components of septoplasty, turbinate reduction and nasal valve repair in one patient.[8] A study of an ultrasonic bone aspirator for turbinoplasty is part of the related airway literature.[9] A paper on persistent obstruction describes the structural contribution of the upper airway nasal complex.[10]

In the 53-patient series, the most common cause of valve obstruction was previous rhinoplasty (79 percent), followed by nasal trauma (15 percent) and congenital anomaly (6 percent).[2] Overviews describe congenital, traumatic and iatrogenic causes, and distinguish internal from external valve collapse, which are treated differently.[12]

Repair typically uses structural grafts. Reviews describe septal cartilage or bone, ear (auricular) cartilage and rib (costal) cartilage as the main sources, each with its own advantages and donor-site trade-offs, chosen by history, examination and surgical goals.[14] Classical manoeuvres for internal and external valves are decades old, and newer methods include radiofrequency-induced thermotherapy, upper lateral strut grafts, stairstep grafts and valve lift techniques.[6]

Some minimally invasive and in-office procedures have been described for selected patients, avoiding general anaesthesia and operating-room costs, including office-based turbinoplasty, septoplasty and functional rhinoplasty-type techniques.[13] Surgeons also describe approaches to dynamic nasal collapse, and a small literature covers valve surgery in children with short-term outcomes and complications reported.[17][18]

Diagnosis is clinical, and objective tools such as computational fluid dynamics, airflow and resistance measurements are used to quantify airway disturbance and to assess surgical results.[16] Validated patient-reported scales such as the NOSE scale are increasingly used; the 25-year review notes that more recent studies incorporate such measures and recommends comparison cohorts and standardised objective measures in future studies.[1][7]

An analysis of U.S. Medicare data for CPT code 30465 found that the annual number of nasal valve repairs rose by about 990 percent between 2001 and 2018 (about 611 percent adjusted for enrollment growth). Total reimbursement rose about 2,026 percent, while the average cost per procedure rose about 38 percent. Most providers in 2013-2018 were otolaryngologists working in facility settings.[15]
A meta-analysis examined whether antibiotic prophylaxis after rhinoplasty is associated with fewer complications.[11]

The 25-year systematic review screened 861 citations and included 44 studies, most graded level 4 and two level 2b; all generally supported the effectiveness of functional rhinoplasty techniques for obstruction from nasal valve collapse.[1]

In the retrospective series of 53 adults followed at least a year, all 12 patients with external valve dysfunction improved, 13 of 14 with combined external and internal dysfunction improved (93 percent), and 24 of 27 with internal valve dysfunction improved (89 percent). Spreader grafts were used in 79 percent and alar batten grafts in 36 percent.[2] A minimally invasive repair has been evaluated with the NOSE scale,[7] and a single-patient computational model assessed individual surgical components of septoplasty, turbinate reduction and valve repair.[8] Review authors note a paucity of controlled trials identifying the most effective method.[5]
